title: Bed & Sleeping Area Organization
subtitle: Two minutes in the morning, and a room that lets you sleep.
objectives: Make a bed correctly, in order
Name the layers of bedding and what each one does
State how often bedding should be changed and why
Explain what makes a sleeping area good for sleeping
Explain how light, temperature and screens affect sleep

cards.title: The cheapest win in the whole room
cards.text: Making a bed takes about two minutes and changes how the entire room reads. Nothing else in this subject pays back that fast.

cards.title: A bed is four layers, in one order
cards.text: Once you know the order it stops being a chore and becomes a sequence you can do half asleep.
points: **Fitted sheet** — the one with elastic corners.
**Flat sheet** — patterned side facing down.
**Blanket or duvet** — on top of the flat sheet.
**Pillows** — last, on top of everything.

cards.title: Four steps, tapped through
cards.text: Two quiz questions come straight from this.

question.text: Put the layers of a made bed in order, from the mattress up.
question.explain: Fitted, flat, blanket, pillows. The flat sheet's edge folds back over the blanket at the top.

cards.title: Far corners first
cards.text: The one piece of technique in the whole job. Doing the two far corners first means you never have to walk round twice.
points: **Two far corners**, then the two near ones.
**Pull the sheet tight** before the last corner.
**Fold the flat sheet back** over the blanket edge.
**That fold** is why the blanket never touches your face.

cards.title: It is a warm-up for the day
cards.text: Coaches start every session the same way for a reason. A short, identical opening tells your brain what is about to happen.
points: **Same action, same order, every morning.**
**It is one finished thing** before anything else starts.
**Cost: two minutes.** Return: the whole room.
**Small completed jobs** make the next one easier.

cards.title: How often bedding gets changed
cards.text: You spend around a third of your life in it, and you sweat and shed skin the whole time.
points: **Sheets and pillowcases:** about once a week.
**More often** in hot weather or after illness.
**Pillowcases matter most** for skin on your face.
**Air the bed** for a few minutes before making it.

question.text: How often should sheets and pillowcases be changed?
question.explain: Weekly. You spend a third of your life in them, sweating and shedding skin the whole time.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: The bed is made. Part 2 is the rest of the room, and whether it lets you sleep. Your place is saved.

cards.title: A bedroom has one job it cannot fail at
cards.text: It can be a place to work, game and store things. But if it stops being a place you sleep well, everything else gets harder.

cards.title: Dark, cool and quiet
cards.text: These three do more for sleep than anything you can buy, and all three are free to change.
points: **Dark** — light tells your body it is daytime.
**Cool** — a slightly cool room helps you fall asleep.
**Quiet** — or at least consistent, unchanging sound.
**Your body reads the room** before you decide anything.

cards.title: Screens delay the signal to sleep
cards.text: Bright light late in the evening pushes back the hormone that starts sleep. The room decides part of that for you.
points: **Melatonin** is the signal that makes you sleepy.
**Bright light suppresses it**, so sleep starts later.
**Charge the phone across the room**, not on the bed.
**Around nine hours** is normal at your age.

question.text: Why do screens late at night make it harder to fall asleep?
options: Bright light suppresses melatonin, the signal to sleep
question.explain: Melatonin starts the process. Bright light tells your body it is still daytime and delays it.

cards.title: Keep the bed for sleeping
cards.text: If everything happens on the bed, your brain stops treating it as the place sleep happens.
points: **Homework at a desk**, not on the bed.
**Clear surfaces near the bed.** Nothing to scan.
**Tomorrow's kit out** before you get in.
**One job per place** makes both jobs easier.

cards.title: A save point is a real place
cards.text: Games separate where you fight from where you rest, and you never confuse the two. A bedroom works the same way.
points: **One space, one purpose.**
**Mixing them makes both worse.**
**Desk for work. Bed for sleep.**
**Even a metre of separation** does the job.

question.text: A slightly cool room helps you fall asleep more easily than a warm one.
question.explain: True. Dark, cool and quiet are the three free changes that do the most for sleep.

terms.def: The sheet with elastic corners that goes directly on the mattress.
The loose sheet above the fitted one, folded back over the blanket at the top.
Leaving bedding open for a few minutes before making the bed.
The hormone that signals sleep. Bright light late at night suppresses it.
The habits and conditions that make good sleep more likely.
Keeping the bed for sleeping so your brain still associates the two.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Fitted, flat, blanket, pillows.** Far corners first.
**Change sheets about once a week.**
**Dark, cool and quiet** are the three free levers.
**Keep the bed for sleeping.** One job per place.

quiz.text: Put the bedding layers in order, from the mattress upward.
quiz.explain: Fitted first, flat sheet next with the pattern face down, then the blanket, then the pillows.
quiz.objective: Make a bed correctly, in order

quiz.text: Which sheet goes directly onto the mattress?
quiz.explain: The fitted sheet, the one with elastic corners. Do the two far corners first.
quiz.objective: Name the layers of bedding and what each one does

quiz.text: Why is the flat sheet folded back over the blanket at the top?
options: So the blanket does not touch your face
To make the bed look longer
To hold the pillows in place
To keep the fitted sheet tight
quiz.explain: That fold is the whole reason the flat sheet exists, and it is why the pattern ends up showing.
quiz.objective: Name the layers of bedding and what each one does

quiz.text: Which corners of a fitted sheet should you do first?
quiz.explain: Far corners first means you never have to walk round the bed twice.
quiz.objective: Make a bed correctly, in order

quiz.text: How often should bed sheets be changed?
quiz.explain: Weekly, and more often in hot weather or after illness.
quiz.objective: State how often bedding should be changed and why

quiz.text: Why does bedding need changing regularly?
options: You sweat and shed skin in it for about a third of your life
Sheets shrink if left too long
It makes the bed easier to make
quiz.explain: A third of your life, every night. Pillowcases matter most because your face is on them.
quiz.objective: State how often bedding should be changed and why

quiz.text: What are the three conditions that most help sleep?
quiz.explain: All three are free to change, and together they beat anything you could buy.
quiz.objective: Explain what makes a sleeping area good for sleeping

quiz.text: What is the hormone that signals your body to sleep?
quiz.explain: Melatonin. Bright light late in the evening suppresses it and pushes sleep later.
quiz.objective: Explain how light, temperature and screens affect sleep

quiz.text: Using a bright screen right before bed makes it harder to fall asleep.
quiz.explain: True. The light suppresses melatonin, so the signal to sleep arrives later than it should.
quiz.objective: Explain how light, temperature and screens affect sleep

quiz.text: Where is the best place to charge a phone overnight?
options: Across the room, away from the bed
quiz.explain: Out of reach means it is not the last or first thing you look at. That is the point of it.
quiz.objective: Explain how light, temperature and screens affect sleep

quiz.text: Why keep homework off the bed?
options: So your brain still treats the bed as the place sleep happens
Because beds are uncomfortable to write on
Because it makes the room untidy
quiz.explain: One job per place. If everything happens on the bed, it stops being a signal for sleep.
quiz.objective: Explain what makes a sleeping area good for sleeping

quiz.text: Making the bed is mainly about how the room looks to other people.
quiz.explain: False. Two minutes for one finished thing before the day starts. It changes how the room reads to you.
quiz.objective: Make a bed correctly, in order

teacher.summary: Week 4 TLE covers bed and sleeping area organisation, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The first half is a procedure, and it is taught as one: the bedLayers figure shows the four layers in order because this is a skill nobody is ever actually shown, only told to do. The far-corners-first detail is included because it is the single piece of technique that makes the job quick. The second half is sleep hygiene, framed around three free levers — dark, cool, quiet — and the melatonin mechanism, which gives a reason rather than a rule. The one-job-per-place idea links back to Week 2's blocks and forward to Week 5's storage: a space with one purpose is easier to use than a space with four.
discussion: Ask him to make the bed once while narrating the four layers. Saying them aloud once fixes the order.
Ask what his room is currently for. Most bedrooms are doing four jobs, and naming them is the start of fixing it.
Ask where the phone charges. It is the single highest-leverage change in this lesson.
Ask what a bad night's sleep costs him the next day, specifically. Training and school both have honest answers.
teacher.extension: Have him move the phone charger across the room for one week and note how long it takes to fall asleep each night. It is a one-variable experiment with his own data.
misconceptions: 'The flat sheet goes pattern side up.' It goes face down, because the top edge folds back over the blanket.
'Bedding only needs changing when it looks dirty.' About once a week. Most of what accumulates is invisible.
'A warm room helps you sleep.' A slightly cool room is easier to fall asleep in.
'Making the bed is about appearances.' It is two minutes for one completed job before the day starts.
